analyses.title: Navigating the Digital World as Humans Do: Universal Visual Grounding for GUI Agents
analyses.research_question: Can a GUI agent relying only on screenshots and pixel-level actions achieve robust cross-platform operation when a specialized model grounds diverse referring expressions directly to interface coordinates?
analyses.methodology: The authors synthesize training triplets consisting of a GUI screenshot, a referring expression, and the target element coordinates, with the expected output defined as the element center point. They build UGround from a slightly adapted LLaVA-style visual grounding architecture and integrate it into the vision-only SeeAct-V agent framework, where an external multimodal planner produces textual plans and UGround maps those plans to screen coordinates. The approach is evaluated on grounding, offline-agent, and online-agent benchmarks spanning web, desktop, and mobile environments, with additional data-scale and referring-expression ablations.

key_findings.finding: On ScreenSpot in the standard grounding setting, the original UGround achieved 73.3 average accuracy versus 53.4 for SeeClick.
With GPT-4o-generated referring expressions in the ScreenSpot agent setting, UGround achieved 81.4 average grounding accuracy versus 52.3 for SeeClick.
Web-derived synthetic grounding data generalized across platforms, including desktop interfaces that were absent from the original UGround training data.
With only 50,000 training screenshots, representing about 600,000 elements, UGround already exceeded SeeClick by more than 10 percentage points in the reported scaling study.
Including positional referring expressions improved ScreenSpot grounding relative to removing positional referring expressions, especially in the standard setting.
key_findings.section: Appendix C.3, Tables C.3 and C.4

key_findings.finding: SeeAct-V agents using UGround were competitive with or better than prior agents on multiple offline and online benchmarks despite using screenshots rather than HTML or accessibility-tree observations for grounding.

limitations: The training corpus is extremely large and contains repeated or similar web elements, leaving substantial room for better data efficiency and deduplication.
Long-tail mobile and desktop interface elements remain under-addressed.
The original training mixture contains no desktop UI screenshots, which the authors identify as a limitation on desktop performance.
UGround requires an external planner and is not a standalone GUI agent.

The evaluated grounding target is a coordinate on a current GUI screenshot; the study does not evaluate cross-version document-element lineage, version identity, or hierarchical page-region-cell provenance.
raw_claims: UGround maps textual referring expressions for GUI elements directly to pixel coordinates.
The training data contains about 10 million GUI elements and referring expressions over about 1.3 million screenshots.
The synthetic grounding examples are generated primarily from webpages.
SeeAct-V separates planning from visual grounding and uses screenshots as its environmental observation.
UGround reached 73.3 average accuracy on the original ScreenSpot standard evaluation.
UGround reached 81.4 average accuracy with GPT-4o planner-generated referring expressions on ScreenSpot.
Training on web screenshots produced substantial transfer to mobile and desktop interfaces.
The data-scaling experiment showed strong results even with 50,000 training screenshots.
Positional referring expressions provide measurable grounding benefit.
The authors identify repetitive training data, long-tail elements, missing desktop training data, and dependence on an external planner as limitations.

analyses.title: Doc-V*: Coarse-to-Fine Interactive Visual Reasoning for Multi-Page Document VQA
analyses.research_question: Can an OCR-free document agent improve long multi-page visual question answering by actively navigating from coarse document overviews to selectively retrieved high-resolution evidence rather than consuming all pages or a fixed retrieval set?
analyses.methodology: Doc-V* formulates multi-page document VQA as a sequential decision process in which a Qwen2.5-VL-based agent first observes global page thumbnails and then chooses among semantic page retrieval, direct page fetching, and final-answer actions while maintaining structured working memory. High-resolution page tokens are cached and injected only when requested, and returned pages retain explicit absolute page identifiers. Training uses supervised fine-tuning on closed-loop expert trajectories followed by GRPO, and evaluation covers five in-domain and out-of-domain document benchmarks using ANLS, F1, and accuracy.

key_findings.finding: The GRPO-trained Doc-V* scored 64.5 on DUDE, 86.2 on MPDocVQA, 77.2 on SlideVQA, 42.1 on MMLongBench-Doc, and 56.3 on LongDocURL, exceeding the corresponding Qwen2.5-VL baseline on every benchmark.
The paper reports an out-of-domain improvement of up to 47.9% over its static RAG baseline.

On MMLongBench-Doc, the full SFT agent achieved 39.8 accuracy while examining 6.4 pages on average; removing retrieval reduced accuracy to 34.9 and increased exploration to 14.2 pages, while removing direct fetching reduced accuracy to 35.2.
Page-level analysis shows complementary behavior: semantic retrieval has higher recall and generally lower precision, while direct page fetching supplies more targeted evidence.
Returned high-resolution page observations are explicitly prefixed with absolute page identifiers, preserving an unambiguous page-to-evidence mapping even when pages are fetched out of order.
Ablating the global thumbnail overview, page-by-page analysis, or working memory degraded performance on all three reported ablation benchmarks.

limitations: All experiments use a single vision-language backbone, Qwen2.5-VL, so backbone generality is not experimentally established.
Evaluation is restricted to single-document scenarios rather than evidence aggregation across multiple heterogeneous documents.
The framework may produce incorrect or incomplete answers because of hallucination or imperfect evidence aggregation.
Evidence provenance is principally page-level: retrieval and fetch actions identify pages, but the framework does not provide evaluated grounding to precise within-page regions or spreadsheet cells.
The study does not model temporal document versions or cross-version element lineage.
raw_claims: Doc-V* treats multi-page document question answering as sequential visual evidence acquisition.
The initial observation contains page thumbnails annotated with absolute page numbers.
The agent can search semantically for pages, fetch pages by absolute index, or terminate with an answer.
High-resolution visual tokens are cached and supplied selectively rather than all at once.
Each returned page is associated with an explicit absolute page identifier.
Training begins with supervised imitation of closed-loop expert trajectories and continues with GRPO.
The raw training data comes from MP-DocVQA and DUDE.
Evaluation uses two in-domain and three out-of-domain document benchmarks.
The GRPO model improved over the direct Qwen2.5-VL baseline on all five reported benchmark columns.
Retrieval and direct fetching are empirically complementary rather than interchangeable.
The authors restrict evaluation to single-document reasoning and one backbone.

analyses.title: Detecting Table Clones and Smells in Spreadsheets
analyses.research_question: Can spreadsheet table clones with corresponding computational semantics, and suspicious inconsistencies among their corresponding cells, be detected automatically from inferred row and column header structure?
analyses.methodology: TableCheck infers row and column headers for cells and uses the derived header information as fingerprints to identify rectangular table blocks whose corresponding cells are likely to have the same or similar computational semantics. It then groups corresponding cells across detected clones and applies outlier-based checks for missing formulas and inconsistent formulas, together with heuristics intended to suppress false positives. The authors evaluate the prototype on 1,617 formula-bearing, Apache-POI-processable spreadsheets from the EUSES corpus, manually validate detected clones and smells, and compare the resulting smells with several prior spreadsheet-analysis techniques.

key_findings.finding: Confirmed table clones occurred in 352 of the 1,617 evaluated spreadsheets, corresponding to 21.8% of the studied formula-bearing spreadsheets.
TableCheck detected 1,317 table-clone groups, of which 1,214 were manually confirmed, yielding 92.2% precision.
Among 3,382 cells flagged as smells, 2,892 were validated as true smells, for 85.5% smell-detection precision.
177 of the 1,214 confirmed table-clone groups contained smells, corresponding to 14.6% of the confirmed clone groups.
Manual inspection found wrong values in 971 of the 2,892 validated smelly cells, or 33.6%.
The strongest compared prior technique detected 35.6% of the 2,892 validated smells found by TableCheck, while the other reported techniques covered still smaller fractions.

The method infers clone correspondence from the present spreadsheet structure rather than recorded copy history; the authors state that detailed version information would be needed to determine how and why clone smells arose.

limitations: TableCheck assumes meaningful row and column headers; missing, incomplete, or mixed headers can prevent effective clone and smell detection.
Changes to headers or insertion and deletion of rows or columns after cloning can cause clones to be missed.
The EUSES corpus may not fully represent spreadsheets used in other populations or domains.
The detected clones and smells were manually checked by the authors rather than by the spreadsheets' original users.
Recall was not measured because exhaustive ground truth for all table clones in EUSES was unavailable.
The authors could not determine how or why individual clone smells arose because the studied corpus lacked detailed version information.
raw_claims: A table clone is defined as rectangular cell blocks whose corresponding cells have the same or similar computational semantics.
TableCheck uses inferred row and column header information as a fingerprint for finding table clones.
Corresponding cells inside detected clone groups are cross-checked for outlying computations.
The experiments use 1,617 EUSES spreadsheets that contain formulas and can be processed by Apache POI.
The authors made their experimental subjects and results available online.
TableCheck detected 1,317 clone groups and validated 1,214 of them.
TableCheck validated 2,892 true smelly cells from 3,382 flagged cells.
A third of the validated smelly cells contained wrong values under the authors' repair-based assessment.
Some clone relationships span different worksheets, so within-sheet-only analyses can miss relevant correspondences.
The paper does not estimate recall because there is no exhaustive clone ground truth for EUSES.
The authors note that ordinary spreadsheets rarely retain metadata identifying which cells originated from copy-and-paste operations.
The lack of detailed version information prevents the study from reconstructing the causes of observed clone inconsistencies.

analyses.title: Document Image Verification Based on Paragraph Alignment and Subtle Change Detection
analyses.research_question: Can document images be verified against stored references by combining paragraph-structure retrieval, geometric paragraph alignment, and contrastive visual comparison robust to print-scan distortions and subtle content changes?
analyses.methodology: The system first segments paragraphs with Faster R-CNN and represents each reference document through structural descriptors including paragraph count, bounding boxes, normalized areas, aspect ratios, and neighboring-paragraph relationships; a four-step matching procedure retrieves candidate references and establishes paragraph correspondences. Matched input paragraphs are geometrically aligned to their reference counterparts, divided into smaller blocks, and compared using a contrastively trained ResNet50 feature extractor, followed by an additional neighborhood-based verification step intended to reject residual misalignment false positives. Experiments use a PubLayNet-derived retrieval database and a second English/Chinese print-scan and tampering database, with retrieval benchmarks, change-detection baselines, and ablations.

key_findings.finding: The proposed structural retrieval method achieved 0.976 precision, 0.96 hit rate, 24.29 ms average retrieval time, and a 1.33 MB retrieval data size in the reported Database A experiment.

With paragraph alignment, the final verification scheme achieved 0.949 precision, 0.978 recall, 0.963 accuracy, and 0.963 F1; removing paragraph alignment reduced precision to 0.725, accuracy to 0.788, and F1 to 0.814 while recall remained 0.975.
At threshold 0.9, adding the secondary verification step increased precision from 0.767 to 0.949 and accuracy from 0.840 to 0.963 while recall remained 0.978.
VGG19 produced a higher precision of 0.976, but the proposed aligned method had substantially higher recall and a higher F1 score, 0.978 and 0.963 versus 0.910 and 0.942.
The approach establishes paragraph-level correspondences independently of OCR text and was evaluated with English and Chinese documents as well as changes affecting text, images, and tables.
Removing position matching from the four-step retrieval procedure reduced retrieval precision from 0.976 to 0.886 while leaving the reported hit rate at 0.96.

limitations: Performance depends on accurate paragraph segmentation, which can be difficult for documents with highly variable or uncommon content types.
The comparison remains sensitive to feature mismatch caused by geometric distortion.
Rotation of the input document relative to its reference can degrade detection performance.
The paper's constructed datasets are not readily available because the authors state that the data are part of an ongoing study.

The system compares an input document against candidate reference images and detects changed content, but it does not evaluate longitudinal multi-version lineage or provenance graphs across a sequence of revisions.
raw_claims: The verification pipeline has a reference-retrieval stage followed by a content-change-detection stage.
Paragraph structure rather than recognized text is used to retrieve candidate reference document images.
The structural descriptor includes paragraph geometry and neighborhood information.
The retrieval procedure also establishes paragraph correspondences between the input and candidate references.
Paragraph alignment is performed before fine-grained block comparison.
A contrastively trained ResNet50 representation is used to distinguish genuine and changed blocks under print-scan distortions.
A second verification pass examines neighboring regions to reduce false positives caused by residual misalignment.
Database A includes 20,000 reference document images selected from PubLayNet for retrieval testing.
Database B contains English and Chinese documents and includes print-scan and deliberately modified samples.
The final aligned configuration reports 0.963 accuracy and 0.963 F1.
The authors report that paragraph alignment is important for avoiding false modification detections caused by spatial mismatch.
The study's constructed datasets are not presently released because they are part of ongoing work.

analyses.title: Class-Agnostic Region-of-Interest Matching in Document Images
analyses.research_question: Can a visual prompt marking an arbitrary region in one document be used to identify semantically corresponding regions in another document without predefined classes or fixed granularity?
analyses.methodology: The authors construct RoI-Matching-Bench from six existing document datasets and organize it into three difficulty levels ranging from visually and positionally similar forms to document pairs differing substantially in appearance and position; Level II includes manual semantic annotation. RoI-Matcher uses a Siamese network to extract multi-level features from reference and target images and cross-attention to integrate and align semantically corresponding features, with an efficient FPNC/grid-sampling design, pre-masking, and PAN-style optimization. It is evaluated using pixel-level mIoU and instance-level F-measure against cross-domain few-shot segmentation and multimodal-language-model baselines, with extensive component ablations.

key_findings.finding: RoI-Matcher achieved 87.3% overall mIoU and 83.9% overall F-measure on RoI-Matching-Bench.
Performance remained strongest across all three benchmark levels, with 92.1% mIoU and 92.2% F-measure at Level I and 85.0% mIoU and 72.3% F-measure at the more difficult Level III.
The reported overall results exceeded the multimodal-model baselines Qwen2-VL-7B at 57.3% mIoU and 55.3% F-measure and InternVL2.5-8B at 53.2% and 50.5%.
The paper reports inference time of 0.056 seconds per image for RoI-Matcher versus 3.121 seconds per image for Qwen2-VL-7B.
Replacing cross-entropy plus Dice loss with PANLoss raised F-measure from 66.8% to 83.0% in the loss ablation while mIoU changed from 85.4% to 85.9%.
Applying the reference mask before feature-pyramid processing produced 87.3% mIoU and 83.9% F-measure versus 87.1% and 68.4% when masking afterward.

limitations: The current model is one-shot and cannot refine a match through multiple successive visual prompts.
The model is visual-only and incorporates no linguistic information.
Repeated inference over multiple RoIs was not experimentally explored.
The method establishes pairwise visual region correspondence but does not model temporal revision identity, document-version lineage, or a page-region-cell provenance hierarchy.
raw_claims: RoI-Matching takes a reference document, a visual mask identifying the desired region, and a target document as input.
The output is the corresponding target-region mask or bounding region without requiring a predefined semantic class.
The benchmark is assembled from six existing document datasets and divided into three difficulty levels.
The hardest level includes document pairs that differ substantially in both visual appearance and position.
Evaluation includes both pixel-level mIoU and instance-oriented F-measure.
RoI-Matcher extracts reference and target features with a Siamese architecture and aligns them through cross-attention.
RoI-Matcher reached 87.3% overall mIoU and 83.9% overall F-measure.
Its reported localization scores substantially exceed the two evaluated multimodal language-model baselines.
The paper reports much lower per-image inference time for RoI-Matcher than for Qwen2-VL-7B.
Pre-masking preserves substantially more instance-level matching performance than post-masking in the reported ablation.
The authors release implementation code and provide a downloadable RoI-Matching-Bench dataset.
The principal stated limitations are one-shot interaction, lack of linguistic input, and absence of repeated multi-RoI inference.
